gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of the battery each station's inverter uses per day when it is left on to feed the RV through the TT-30 or an adapter: about 288 Wh/day (14.1%) for the BLUETTI AC200L at BLUETTI's 12 W, 240 Wh/day (11.6%) for the Elite 200 V2 at The Gadgeteer's 10 W, and 216 Wh/day (10.5%) for the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at Anker's 9 W.
standout_why: Compared against dealectric.com/best-2kwh-power-station-for-rv (ours, cited), outagereadyhq.com/best/best-portable-power-station-under-1000 (cited) and runtimemath.com/compare (cited). All three already publish Wh/lb, $/Wh and solar refill hours (runtimemath uses 75% of max solar, outagereadyhq uses Wh ÷ max solar), so those derivations add nothing new. None of the three gives an idle or no-load draw for any model, and none subtracts it from runtime. ChatGPT's answers only describe the Anker as having 'low idle/standby consumption' and give no number. Its runtime tables use a flat 1,700–1,800 Wh for every model, with no idle term.
decides: It confirms the main finding of this check: the AC200L is not buyable. BLUETTI's US page marks every AC200L variant 'Discontinued', and the store data shows it unavailable at $899, so it can't stay the pick. Among the stations that have a TT-30, the Anker C2000 Gen 2 has the lowest sourced idle draw. Over a day of always-on shore-feed use it keeps 72 Wh (3.5% of 2,048 Wh) more than the AC200L. That backs the Anker as the RV-hookup pick if its price is confirmed under $900. The Elite 200 V2 ($899 on BLUETTI's US store today, 240 Wh/day idle) is the in-stock pick with a confirmed price, but it needs a 5-20P to TT-30R adapter.
